newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. Mexico envoy slams drug certification policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Mexico envoy slams drug certification policy.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to Mexico on Wednesday criticised the United States' policy of "certifying" other nations' efforts in the drugs war, saying it was counterproductive to stopping the illegal narcotics trade.
"It is a counterproductive method, even if it's well intentioned in the fight against narcotraficking," Ambassador James Jones told the American Chamber of Commerce in Mexico City.

"It could trigger, in my judgment, a wave of responses, a wave of fingerpointing between and among, producing, transiting and consumer nations, and in that atmosphere of accusations the only winners would be the narcotrafickers themselves," Jones said.
The White House recently certified Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs, but Congress has moved to strip certification because of drug corruption in Mexico.

Although U.S. lawmakers would waive potential sanctions against Mexico were it decertified, Mexico has vowed to retaliate if the move wins out. U.S. officials worry that Mexico might do less to cooperate in the drug war instead of more.
Jones has moved quickly to try to defuse rising tensions between the two nations over the process, which Mexico resents as an interference in its affairs.
Earlier this week, Jones said the United States had to shoulder some of the blame for drug trafficking as the world's leading drug consumer.
On Wednesday, the envoy told U.S. businessmen that many U.S. lawmakers agreed with his negative assessment of the certification process.

"One of the things I found last week, in both the House and Senate sides, was a lot of concern among Democrats and Republicans alike that the whole certification process should be reviewed; some people believe it should be entirely scrapped," he said.

Although certification is an annual process that ruffles feathers in nations such as Mexico and Colombia, this year's process became an explosive issue when Mexico arrested its top anti-drugs official in February on drug corruption charges.
U.S. lawmakers said it proved corruption ran high into Mexico's government, which defended itself by saying it was doing everything it could to root out corruption.
